en: The *Brahmacārin Kṛṣṇa Sūtra*, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling along the banks of the Nairañjanā River and stayed there for one month.

He performed the eighteen transformations, converting the three Kāśyapa brothers and their thousand disciples; he then traveled on to the city of Rājagṛha, where he stayed for one year, instructing the people of the kingdom and preaching the Dharma for them.
Two years after first attaining the Way of Buddhahood, he arrived at Śrāvastī to propagate his teachings and deliver gods, humans, and the people of the world.
At that time, there was a brahmin on Mount Gandhamādana named Kāla, who had attained the four dhyānas and was endowed with the five supernormal powers:
the power of clairvoyance, the power of clairaudience, the power of flying through the air, the power of knowing the thoughts of others, and the power of knowing the future rebirths of men.
He expounded the meaning of the sutras, moving Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the various spirits, ghosts, and nāgas, as well as King Yama, all of whom went to listen to him;
his speech was elegant and sublime, his voice harmonious like that of Brahmā, and they consulted and received his teachings day after day without weariness;
his voice reached far and wide, and all came to seek refuge in his teaching.
At that time, King Yama sat listening to the Dharma, his tears falling like rain; looking up and gazing about, he sighed with even greater sorrow.
Then the brahmin asked King Yama:
"Why do you weep, your tears falling like rain?"
Yama replied: "Matters must return to their reality; one must not speak falsely.
You have now preached the sutra with eloquent and skillful words; its principles are most wonderful, like a lotus flower or a bright moon pearl."
Yet my life is drawing to a close, with only seven days remaining; fearing that they may suddenly pass away as I enter the next world, I weep with such grief that I cannot restrain myself.
Furthermore, when you passed away, you fell into hell within my realm.
Now that you have come to me of your own accord and received the Dharma with a single mind, I shall subject you to the fivefold torments of interrogation and torture.
Reflecting deeply upon this, my grief increased beyond all measure; it is impossible to describe.
The Brahmin was struck with astonishment; his mind filled with contemplation, he replied to King Yama:
“I attained the four dhyānas and perfected the five supernormal powers; I walked alone through the four regions and ascended to the Brahma Heaven without hindrance.”
"Since there is no fault or transgression, for what reason should one fall into the realm of Yama?

King Yama replied, "When you were approaching the end of your life, you encountered an adversary; you gave rise to anger and resentment, intending to cause harm, and thereby lost the meaning of your original practice. For this reason, you have gone to the realm of Yama."
Upon hearing this, the brahmin was suddenly overcome with despondency; he did not know what plan to devise or what expedient to employ to escape this peril.
He was filled with grief and bewilderment, his heart as if immersed in boiling water or fire, restless whether sitting or rising, and he let out long sighs.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, and the various deities asked,
"Why do you sigh so deeply and restlessly?
The brahmin replied:
"My life is coming to an end, with only seven days remaining; moreover, an evil adversary shall come to disturb my virtuous mind, and for this reason, I fear returning to the woeful realms."
"For this reason, he tosses and turns, unable to overcome his distress.
At that time, there were various benevolent deities on Mount Gandhamādana who frequently visited the Buddha’s dwelling to inquire about and receive the scriptures; they said to the brahmin:
"The Buddha has appeared in the world; do you not know of it?"
The brahmin replied, "I am but an ordinary person; how could I possibly know this?
The spirit spoke again:

“The Buddha is the savior of all within the three realms; he delivers those not yet delivered, liberates those not yet liberated, and brings peace to those not yet at peace, rescuing all from peril and distress and leading them to the Way of eternal stillness and non-action.”
"Why do you not go to the Buddha?
You may thereby be liberated from suffering and affliction, attain eternal tranquility, and find harmony with the Way and its Virtue.

Upon hearing this, the Brahmin leaped for joy as if one seeing light in the darkness; he took branches of the *wutong* and *hehuan* trees—trees of exquisite color—with both hands and flew to where the Buddha was.
Before he had even arrived, the Buddha told Māyī:
"The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate and cultivates boundless pity;
he has never forgotten or abandoned those who ought to be delivered."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The tides follow the course of the cliffs, Never overstepping their ancient bounds;
Should a water spirit cause disorder, It would rise to violate the established flow."
“The Buddha contemplates that which is originally non-existent;
observing those who should be delivered, he enables them all to attain liberation and salvation, never failing or erring.
Thereupon, the brahmin flew to where the Buddha was, staying in mid-air, and turned directly toward the Buddha in homage.
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Kāla, saying:
"Let go! Let go!"
The brahmin assented, saying,
"As the World-Honored One has instructed.
He immediately relinquished the *ficus religiosa* tree on his right hand and planted it on the Buddha's right side.
He further said to the brahmin:
"Let go! Let go!"
The brahmin immediately released the *aśoka* tree held in his left hand and planted it on the Buddha’s left side.
The Buddha spoke again: “Release it!”
"Relinquish them!
The brahmin replied, "I have just left two trees on either side of the Buddha; standing here empty-handed, what more could I relinquish?"
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"The Buddha does not say that you have relinquished the object in your hand.

What the Buddha calls 'relinquishing' means that one must relinquish what precedes, relinquish what follows, and also relinquish what is in between, so that there is no place of abiding; only then will one cross over the perils and afflictions of birth and death."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"One should abandon its root, and one should also abandon its branches;
when there is no dwelling place in between, one then crosses over the source of birth and death."
Within, there are no six sense bases; externally, the decays cannot advance.
By setting aside the six emotions, one then achieves the swiftness of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
Upon hearing what the Buddha had said, the Brahmin Kāla thought to himself:
"When one does not perceive a self, one realizes that the mind is non-existent.
Since the mind is fundamentally non-existent, one administers medicine according to the illness, and the base mind is opened and liberated.
It is like a blind person regaining their sight or a deaf person regaining their hearing; this is truly universal vision, the thorough examination of all-knowledge."
"Now that he has encountered the Buddha, his virtue is beyond measure.
He immediately descended, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, responding to the fundamental intent of his mind, gave a detailed exposition, revealing the site of enlightenment and expounding upon the three gates of liberation.
At that time, he immediately abided in the stage of non-retrogression, free from all sorrow and affliction. Praising the Buddha’s merits, he spoke in verse:
“His radiance surpasses the sun and moon; His wisdom is like the great ocean.
With great compassion and boundless pity, The ten directions all rejoice and revere him.”
Sentient beings flow through the three realms for countless billions of years;
To cure their ailments, you bestow the medicine of the Dharma, Proclaiming your great eloquence.
Though you manifest entry into birth and death, You circulate therein without coming or going.
Exhort and transform others to be diligent; neither sin nor merit can be substituted for one another.
Strive with effort and diligence; do not be ravaged by desire.
Subdue and eliminate the four maras of decline; when the Way is perfected, there will be no hindrance.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
"I have been lost in delusion for a very long time!
I pray that you will show me compassion and allow me to become a śramaṇa!"
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.
His hair fell away of its own accord, the kāṣāya robe clothed his body, and his deportment became perfectly composed;
he thus became a śramaṇa. He went to King Yama and said to him:
"You originally thought that my remaining life span was seven days and that I would fall into hell.

Now, having become a śramaṇa, I am fully endowed with supernormal powers; all outflows are exhausted, I have crossed over the four great rivers, and all ailments are forever eliminated, like being within a vast protective enclosure."
At that time, his lifespan increased by seven times seven days;
all sufferings were extinguished, and he surpassed the methods of external heterodox arts.
He dwelt freely in the world for further incalculable kalpas.
King Yama replied:

"By virtue of the remaining merit you relied upon, you were able to encounter the Buddha. At that time, he bestowed the Dharma according to your illness, extinguishing lust, anger, and delusion; you have fully perfected the supernormal powers and are free from doubt regarding both the internal and external."
Were it otherwise, one would be like a mouse encountering a wildcat, or like rice struck by calamity, dragged away by sin;
like a fish caught on a hook and bait, one would fall into hell with no time of release in sight.
"Now that we have been forever liberated, let us rejoice in one another’s stead.
When these words were spoken, countless people all resolved their minds upon the Way.
Thus spoke the Buddha; the bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, the ascetic Kāśyapa, devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, and worldly people were all filled with joy, and having paid their respects, they departed.
The Sūtra on the Brahmin Kāḷāma Spoken by the Buddha.
